destinations.name: Spiti Valley
destinations.lead: A cold mountain desert of whitewashed monasteries, fossil villages and rivers the colour of glacier-melt.
destinations.overview:
Spiti — literally “the middle land” between India and Tibet — is a high-altitude desert valley cradled in the trans-Himalaya. Days are sharp and blue, nights bitterly clear, and the few villages clinging to its slopes are among the highest inhabited places on earth.

It is raw, remote and slow to reach, which is exactly the point. You come for thousand-year-old gompas, for the silence between two ridgelines, and for a night sky so dense with stars it feels close enough to touch.
destinations.secSeason:
The valley is realistically open from mid-May to mid-October, once Kunzum Pass clears of snow. June to September are the warmest, safest months. By late October the passes begin to close and the Manali route shuts for winter.

Winter Spiti (via Shimla–Kinnaur) is possible for hardy travellers — frozen, severe and beautiful, with the chance of spotting snow leopard.
destinations.secReach:
Two roads lead in. The Shimla–Kinnaur approach (via Reckong Peo and Nako) stays open most of the year and helps you acclimatise gradually. The Manali–Kunzum La approach is shorter and more dramatic but summer-only.

Nearest airport: Bhuntar (Kullu). Nearest railhead: Shimla or Chandigarh. Most travellers hire a shared cab or self-drive a sturdy SUV.
destinations.secStay: Expect homestays and small guesthouses rather than hotels. Kaza is the main base with the most options; villages like Kibber, Langza, Komic and Demul run warm, simple homestays — the best way to meet Spiti and support its families.
destinations.secTravel: There is a skeletal local bus network, but the most reliable way around is a hired vehicle with a local driver who knows the road and the altitude. Distances look short on the map but are slow on the ground.
destinations.secActivities:
• Monastery circuit — Key, Dhankar, Tabo and Komic
  • Stargazing and astrophotography from Langza or Kibber
  • Short acclimatised treks and village walks
  • Spotting blue sheep, ibex and (in winter) snow leopard
  • The world’s highest post office at Hikkim
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Key Monastery — the iconic hillside gompa
  • Dhankar — a fort-monastery on a cliff edge
  • Tabo — the 1,000-year-old “Ajanta of the Himalayas”
  • Chandratal Lake — the crescent-moon lake near Kunzum La
  • Langza — Buddha statue, fossils and peak views
destinations.secNotes: Altitude is the real challenge — build in a day or two to acclimatise and drink plenty of water. Carry cash; ATMs are scarce. Mobile coverage is limited (BSNL/Jio postpaid works best). Pack layers for sub-zero nights even in summer, and respect monastery etiquette.
destinations.extItinerary:
A classic 8-day Spiti loop, taking the gentler Shimla–Kinnaur road in (better for acclimatising) and exiting via Manali.

  • Day 1–2: Shimla → Sangla / Chitkul, easing up in altitude
  • Day 3: Chitkul → Nako → Tabo — the first Spiti monasteries
  • Day 4: Tabo → Dhankar → Pin Valley
  • Day 5: Kaza base — Key, Kibber, Hikkim & Komic
  • Day 6: Langza, Lalung and Demul villages
  • Day 7: Kaza → Chandratal over Kunzum La
  • Day 8: Chandratal → Manali via Rohtang
destinations.extFood:
Spiti food is hearty, warming and Tibetan-influenced:

  • Thukpa — a noodle soup that fixes any cold day
  • Momos — steamed dumplings, veg or mutton
  • Butter tea & chhang — salted tea and a local barley brew
  • Tsampa — roasted barley flour, the everyday staple
  • Seabuckthorn juice — tart, vitamin-rich and grown locally
destinations.extCulture: Spiti is devoutly Tibetan-Buddhist, and its monasteries are living centres of community life. Walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels, ask before photographing monks or shrine interiors, and dress modestly inside the gompas. If your timing aligns, the Losar (Tibetan New Year) celebrations and monastery Chaam mask dances are unforgettable.
destinations.extBudget:
Spiti is cheap on the ground but transport-heavy.

  • Homestays: ₹800–1,500 a night, usually with meals
  • Meals: ₹150–300 a plate
  • The vehicle: your biggest cost — budget for fuel and a reliable driver
  • Daily budget: roughly ₹2,000–3,500 per person, excluding the cab
destinations.extFaq:
Is Spiti safe for first-time high-altitude travellers?
Yes — if you acclimatise gradually (enter from the Shimla side) and watch for symptoms of altitude sickness.

Do I need permits?
Indian nationals don't; foreign nationals need an Inner Line Permit for the border stretches, easily arranged en route.

Are there ATMs and mobile network?
Limited — only BSNL/Jio postpaid works around Kaza, and ATMs are unreliable, so carry cash.

destinations.name: Ladakh
destinations.lead: Moonscape passes, turquoise high-altitude lakes and Tibetan-Buddhist monasteries under an enormous sky.
destinations.overview:
Ladakh is a high desert plateau of the western Himalaya — bare ochre mountains, prayer-flag passes and rivers running green and grey. Leh, its capital, sits at 3,500 m and is the gateway to a region the size of a small country.

This is big-sky, big-silence travel: gompas perched on crags, road trips over some of the highest motorable passes on earth, and lakes so blue they look unreal.
destinations.secSeason: The classic window is May to September, when the Manali and Srinagar roads are open and the lakes are ice-free. September and October bring golden light and thinner crowds. Winter is snowbound but magical — the season of the Chadar frozen-river trek.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Leh (IXL) — simplest, but rest the first day to acclimatise. Overland, the Srinagar–Leh and Manali–Leh highways are spectacular two-day drives, open roughly June to October.
destinations.secStay: Leh has everything from backpacker guesthouses to boutique hotels. For Nubra and Pangong, expect homestays and seasonal tented camps. Local guesthouses keep you closer to Ladakhi life.
destinations.secTravel: Hire a cab or rent a motorcycle (a Royal Enfield is a rite of passage). Inner Line Permits are required for Nubra, Pangong and Tso Moriri — easily arranged in Leh.
destinations.secActivities:
• Road trip to Pangong Tso and Nubra over Khardung La
  • Monastery-hopping — Thiksey, Hemis, Diskit, Lamayuru
  • River rafting on the Zanskar and Indus
  • Double-humped camel rides on the Hunder dunes
  • Winter: the Chadar trek on the frozen Zanskar
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Pangong Tso — the colour-shifting lake on the Tibet border
  • Nubra Valley — dunes, monasteries and the Shyok river
  • Thiksey Monastery — a mini-Potala at dawn
  • Khardung La — one of the world’s highest motorable passes
  • Magnetic Hill & Sangam — the Indus–Zanskar confluence
destinations.secNotes: Spend 24–48 hours acclimatising in Leh before heading higher. Stay hydrated, avoid alcohol early on, and carry strong sunscreen — UV at altitude is fierce. Only postpaid SIMs work, and not everywhere.
destinations.extItinerary:
A well-paced 7-day Ladakh circuit from Leh, with a vital acclimatisation day up front.

  • Day 1: Arrive Leh — rest and acclimatise
  • Day 2: Leh monasteries — Shey, Thiksey, Hemis
  • Day 3: Leh → Nubra Valley over Khardung La
  • Day 4: Nubra — Hunder dunes & Diskit monastery
  • Day 5: Nubra → Pangong Tso
  • Day 6: Pangong → Leh
  • Day 7: Sham Valley — Magnetic Hill, Sangam, Alchi
destinations.extFood:
Ladakhi food is simple, filling mountain fare:

  • Skyu & chutagi — pasta-and-root-vegetable stews
  • Momos and thukpa — the Himalayan staples
  • Apricots — fresh, dried and as jam, everywhere in season
  • Butter tea & chhang — salted tea and barley beer
  • Khambir — local Ladakhi bread
destinations.extCulture: Ladakh blends Tibetan-Buddhist and Muslim cultures. Spin prayer wheels clockwise, remove shoes and cover up in monasteries, and ask before photographing people. Time your trip with the masked Hemis Festival (summer) or the September Ladakh Festival for music, dance and polo.
destinations.extBudget:
• Guesthouses: ₹1,000–2,500 a night in Leh
  • Motorcycle rental: ₹1,200–1,800 a day for a Royal Enfield
  • Permits: a small per-day fee for Nubra/Pangong
  • Daily budget: ₹2,500–4,000 per person, more if you hire a private cab
destinations.extFaq:
How do I avoid altitude sickness?
Rest fully on day one, hydrate, skip alcohol early, and ascend gradually before tackling the high passes.

Which permits do I need?
Inner Line (Indians) or Protected Area (foreigners) permits for Nubra, Pangong and Tso Moriri — arranged in minutes in Leh.

Will my phone work?
Only postpaid SIMs work in Ladakh, and coverage thins out beyond Leh.

destinations.name: Andaman Islands
destinations.lead: White-sand beaches, glass-clear water and some of Asia’s best coral reefs in the Bay of Bengal.
destinations.overview:
The Andamans are a chain of tropical islands far out in the Bay of Bengal — closer to Myanmar than mainland India. Think powder-soft beaches, mangrove creeks and warm turquoise shallows teeming with reef life.

Havelock (Swaraj Dweep) and Neil (Shaheed Dweep) are the traveller favourites, while Port Blair holds the islands’ poignant colonial history.
destinations.secSeason: November to April is the sweet spot — calm seas, clear visibility for diving, and dry sunny days. The monsoon (May–September) brings rough water and ferry disruptions, though it has its own green beauty.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Port Blair (IXZ) from Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru or Delhi. From there, fast catamaran ferries reach Havelock and Neil in 1.5–2 hours. Book ferries ahead in peak season.
destinations.secStay: Havelock ranges from beach huts to luxury eco-resorts (the Radhanagar end is prettiest). Neil is quieter and cheaper. Port Blair has practical city hotels for arrival and departure nights.
destinations.secTravel: Ferries link the main islands; on each island, hire a scooter or auto. Government ferries are cheapest; private catamarans are faster and more comfortable.
destinations.secActivities:
• Scuba diving and snorkelling off Havelock and Neil
  • Sunset at Radhanagar Beach (Beach No. 7)
  • Sea-walking and glass-bottom boats for non-divers
  • Kayaking through bioluminescent mangroves
  • History walk at the Cellular Jail, Port Blair
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Radhanagar Beach — rated among Asia’s best
  • Elephant Beach — snorkelling and water sports
  • Natural Bridge, Neil Island
  • Cellular Jail — and its evening light-and-sound show
  • Ross & Smith Islands — a twin-island sandbar
destinations.secNotes: Carry enough cash — ATMs are limited outside Port Blair. Mobile coverage is patchy (Airtel/BSNL best). Respect tribal-reserve restrictions and reef etiquette: no touching coral, reef-safe sunscreen only.
destinations.extItinerary:
A relaxed 6-day island-hop covering history, beaches and reefs.

  • Day 1: Port Blair — Cellular Jail & the evening light show
  • Day 2: Ferry to Havelock — sunset at Radhanagar
  • Day 3: Havelock — diving or snorkelling at Elephant Beach
  • Day 4: Neil Island — Natural Bridge & Bharatpur Beach
  • Day 5: Back to Port Blair — Ross Island
  • Day 6: Departure
destinations.extFood:
It's all about the sea here:

  • Grilled & curried fish — caught that morning
  • Coconut prawn curry — a local favourite
  • Lobster and crab — at the beach shacks on Havelock
  • Tropical fruit — pineapple, papaya, fresh coconut water
  • Mainland classics — the islands' settler mix means good Bengali and South-Indian food too
destinations.extCulture: The Andamans are a melting pot of settlers — Bengali, Tamil, Telugu and more — with a famously easy island pace. The islands are also home to protected indigenous tribes: the Jarawa reserve is strictly off-limits, with no contact or photography permitted. Respect reef and beach rules everywhere.
destinations.extBudget:
• Stays: ₹1,500–4,000 (beach huts to eco-resorts)
  • Ferries: ₹1,000–1,500 each way between islands
  • Scuba: ₹3,500–6,000 for a beginner dive
  • Daily budget: ₹3,000–6,000 per person
destinations.extFaq:
Do I need to book ferries in advance?
Yes — private catamarans to Havelock and Neil sell out in peak season, so book ahead.

Is diving suitable for beginners?
Absolutely — "Discover Scuba" intro dives need no certification and are very popular here.

How's connectivity?
Patchy outside Port Blair (Airtel/BSNL are best), so carry cash too.

destinations.name: Manali & Kasol
destinations.lead: Pine-clad valleys, snow runs and riverside cafés — the Himalayas at their most easy-going.
destinations.overview:
Manali and the nearby Parvati Valley (Kasol, Tosh, Malana) are Himachal’s all-season playground. Manali pairs apple orchards and cedar forests with adventure sport; Kasol is a laid-back riverside hub of cafés and trailheads.

It’s the gentle introduction to the high Himalaya — easy to reach, soft on the lungs, and endlessly scenic.
destinations.secSeason: There’s no wrong time. March–June is pleasant and green; October–February brings snow and winter sport around Solang. The monsoon (July–August) is lush but landslide-prone on mountain roads.
destinations.secReach: Drive or take an overnight Volvo bus from Delhi/Chandigarh (10–14 hrs). Nearest airport: Bhuntar (Kullu), ~50 km away. Nearest railhead: Chandigarh or Joginder Nagar.
destinations.secStay: Manali spans hostels to luxury resorts (Old Manali for cafés, Naggar for quiet heritage stays). Kasol, Tosh and Tirthan offer cosy riverside guesthouses.
destinations.secTravel: Local buses and shared cabs cover the main routes; rent a scooter or bike for the valleys. Many travellers base in Manali and day-trip out.
destinations.secActivities:
• Snow play and skiing at Solang and Gulaba
  • Paragliding, Beas-river rafting and zip-lining
  • Treks to Kheerganga, Tosh and Chandrakhani
  • Café-hopping along the Parvati river in Kasol
  • Day trips through the Atal Tunnel to Lahaul
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Solang Valley — adventure-sport hub
  • Hadimba Temple — cedar-forest shrine
  • Atal Tunnel — gateway to Lahaul
  • Kheerganga — hot springs at the trek’s end
  • Naggar Castle — heritage and the Roerich gallery
destinations.secNotes: Mountain roads slow in monsoon and heavy snow — keep the itinerary flexible. The Atal Tunnel keeps Lahaul accessible even in winter. Respect local customs in Malana, and don’t leave litter on the trails.
destinations.extItinerary:
A flexible 5-day mix of Manali and the Parvati Valley.

  • Day 1: Arrive Manali — Hadimba Temple & Old Manali cafés
  • Day 2: Solang Valley, Atal Tunnel & Sissu
  • Day 3: Drive to Kasol, riverside evening
  • Day 4: Kheerganga trek (or Tosh village)
  • Day 5: Naggar Castle en route back
destinations.extFood:
• Siddu — a steamed Himachali bread, best with ghee
  • Trout — fresh from mountain streams
  • Dham — the traditional Himachali festive thali
  • Kasol café food — Israeli plates, wood-fired pizza, big breakfasts
  • Apple cider & local juices
destinations.extCulture: This is Pahari (hill) culture, centred on village temples and apple orchards. The Hadimba and Manu temples are revered; in Malana, respect the village's strict customs and don't touch locals or their belongings without asking. Kullu's Dussehra is a week-long, deity-filled spectacle.
destinations.extBudget:
• Hostels: ₹500–800 a bed
  • Hotels/guesthouses: ₹1,500–4,000
  • Activities: paragliding from ₹2,000, rafting from ₹600
  • Daily budget: ₹1,500–3,000 per person
destinations.extFaq:
When is there snow?
December–February around Solang and Gulaba; the Atal Tunnel keeps Lahaul reachable in winter.

How do I get there?
Overnight Volvo from Delhi/Chandigarh, or fly to Bhuntar (Kullu), ~50 km away.

Is it very crowded?
Peak season and weekends are busy — the Parvati Valley (Tosh, Tirthan) stays calmer.

destinations.name: Kerala Backwaters
destinations.lead: A green labyrinth of palm-fringed canals, lakes and rice paddies, best seen from the deck of a houseboat.
destinations.overview:
The Kerala backwaters are a network of brackish lagoons and canals running parallel to the Arabian Sea coast. Life here moves at the pace of the water — village ferries, coir boats, and slow sunsets over Vembanad Lake.

Alleppey (Alappuzha) and Kumarakom are the classic bases for a houseboat cruise; Kollam and Kuttanad reward those who want quieter waterways.
destinations.secSeason: September to March offers the best weather — green from the rains but dry overhead. The monsoon (June–August) is dramatic and ideal for Ayurveda retreats. Onam (Aug/Sep) brings the spectacular snake-boat races.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Kochi (COK) — about 1.5 hrs from Alleppey. Kottayam and Alappuzha are well connected by train. Most houseboats depart from Alleppey’s Finishing Point.
destinations.secStay: The headline experience is an overnight houseboat (kettuvallam). Pair it with a lakeside homestay or heritage resort in Kumarakom for a night or two on land.
destinations.secTravel: Public ferries are a cheap, scenic way to move between villages. Cabs and autos cover the towns; canoe and shikara rides reach the narrow canals houseboats can’t.
destinations.secActivities:
• Overnight houseboat cruise on Vembanad Lake
  • Sunrise village-canoe tour through the canals
  • Ayurveda massage and wellness treatments
  • Kathakali and Kalaripayattu performances in Kochi
  • Birdwatching at Kumarakom sanctuary
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Vembanad Lake — the heart of the backwaters
  • Alleppey Finishing Point — houseboat harbour
  • Kumarakom Bird Sanctuary
  • Pathiramanal Island
  • Fort Kochi — Chinese nets and colonial lanes
destinations.secNotes: Book houseboats through reputable operators and confirm what’s included. Carry mosquito repellent for evenings on the water. Don’t miss the karimeen (pearl-spot fish) or a traditional sadya served on a banana leaf.
destinations.extItinerary:
A gentle 5-day backwaters-and-coast itinerary.

  • Day 1: Kochi — Fort Kochi, Chinese nets, a Kathakali show
  • Day 2: Transfer to Alleppey — overnight houseboat
  • Day 3: Kumarakom — lakeside village & bird sanctuary
  • Day 4: Ayurveda & a sunrise canoe tour
  • Day 5: Back to Kochi
destinations.extFood:
• Sadya — a vegetarian feast on a banana leaf
  • Karimeen pollichathu — pearl-spot fish grilled in banana leaf
  • Appam with stew — lacy rice pancakes, coconut stew
  • Puttu & kadala — steamed rice cake with black-chickpea curry
  • Malabar parotta — flaky bread with rich curries
destinations.extCulture: Kerala's Malayali culture runs deep in art and ritual — the all-night Kathakali and Theyyam performances, and martial Kalaripayattu. Dress modestly at temples (some restrict non-Hindus), and time a visit with Onam (Aug/Sep) for feasts and snake-boat races.
destinations.extBudget:
• Houseboats: ₹8,000–20,000 a night (shared or private)
  • Homestays/resorts: ₹1,500–3,500
  • Meals: ₹150–400
  • Daily budget: ₹2,500–5,000 per person
destinations.extFaq:
Is a houseboat worth it?
Yes — one overnight is plenty to experience it; pair it with a lakeside stay rather than two nights aboard.

Best time to visit?
September–March for dry weather; the monsoon is ideal for Ayurveda retreats.

Are there good vegetarian options?
Excellent — the sadya alone is a vegetarian highlight of India.

destinations.name: Meghalaya
destinations.lead: The wettest place on earth — living root bridges, plunging waterfalls and India’s clearest river.
destinations.overview:
Meghalaya, “the abode of clouds,” is a land of forested hills, limestone caves and astonishing rainfall. Over generations the Khasi people have trained the roots of rubber-fig trees into living bridges that span jungle rivers.

It’s a place of waterfalls beyond counting, of Cherrapunji and Mawsynram (the rainiest spots on the planet), and of Dawki’s river so clear the boats appear to float on air.
destinations.secSeason: October to May is the dry, comfortable window for trekking and clear-river views. The monsoon (June–September) is when the waterfalls roar at full power — spectacular, but trails turn slippery and leech-ridden.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Guwahati (GAU), Assam, then drive ~3 hrs to Shillong (which also has a small airport at Umroi). From Shillong, hire a cab for Cherrapunji, Dawki and Nongriat.
destinations.secStay: Shillong is the main hotel hub. For the root bridges, stay in a Nongriat or Cherrapunji homestay; for Dawki/Shnongpdeng, riverside camps are the draw.
destinations.secTravel: Shared sumos and hired cabs are the norm — there’s no train into the hills. Reaching Nongriat means a steep stairway trek (around 3,500 steps down and back).
destinations.secActivities:
• Trek to the Double-Decker Living Root Bridge, Nongriat
  • Kayaking or boating on the crystal-clear Umngot river, Dawki
  • Caving in Mawsmai and Arwah caves
  • Chasing waterfalls — Nohkalikai, Seven Sisters, Wei Sawdong
  • Camping at Shnongpdeng under the stars
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Double-Decker Root Bridge, Nongriat
  • Nohkalikai Falls — India’s tallest plunge waterfall
  • Dawki / Umngot River
  • Mawlynnong — “Asia’s cleanest village”
  • Living root bridges around Cherrapunji
destinations.secNotes: The Nongriat trek is strenuous — wear good shoes and carry water. Carry cash; ATMs thin out beyond Shillong. Respect village rules in Mawlynnong, and pack a rain layer year-round — this is cloud country.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 6-day loop through Shillong, Cherrapunji and the clear-water east.

  • Day 1: Guwahati → Shillong (via Umiam Lake)
  • Day 2: Shillong — Elephant Falls, local markets
  • Day 3: Cherrapunji — Nohkalikai Falls & Mawsmai caves
  • Day 4: Trek to the Double-Decker Root Bridge, Nongriat
  • Day 5: Dawki & Mawlynnong village
  • Day 6: Return to Guwahati
destinations.extFood:
• Jadoh — Khasi rice cooked with pork
  • Dohneiiong — pork in black-sesame gravy
  • Tungrymbai — fermented soybean dish
  • Smoked meats — a hill speciality
  • Pukhlein & rice beer — sweet rice fritters and local brew
destinations.extCulture: The Khasi and Garo are among the world's few matrilineal societies — lineage and property pass through the youngest daughter. Villages like Mawlynnong are famously clean and community-run, so follow local rules. Don't miss the Nongkrem and Wangala harvest festivals.
destinations.extBudget:
• Homestays/guesthouses: ₹800–2,000
  • Shared sumos & cabs: the main way to get around
  • Daily budget: ₹1,800–3,500 per person
destinations.extFaq:
Monsoon or dry season?
October–May for trekking and clear rivers; the monsoon brings the waterfalls to full roar but slick, leech-prone trails.

How hard is the Nongriat trek?
Strenuous — around 3,500 steps down and back up; good shoes and water essential.

Is connectivity reliable?
Fine in Shillong, patchy beyond — carry cash past the city.

destinations.name: Jaisalmer & Jodhpur
destinations.lead: The golden desert fort and the blue city — Rajasthan’s most cinematic pairing of sand, stone and colour.
destinations.overview:
Jaisalmer rises from the Thar Desert like a sandcastle — a living fort of honey-coloured stone where families still live within the ramparts. A few hours away, Jodhpur spreads beneath the mighty Mehrangarh Fort, its old town washed in indigo blue.

Together they’re the essence of desert Rajasthan: havelis, camel trails, folk music under the stars, and bazaars heavy with colour and spice.
destinations.secSeason: October to March is the only comfortable time — warm days, cool nights, perfect for the dunes. Summer (April–June) is brutally hot. The Jaisalmer Desert Festival (February) is a highlight.
destinations.secReach: Jodhpur has the nearest major airport (JDH) and a busy railway station. Jaisalmer is reached by overnight train or a 5-hr drive from Jodhpur — the two pair naturally on one trip.
destinations.secStay: Sleep inside Jaisalmer Fort in a heritage haveli, or in a luxury desert camp near the Sam dunes. In Jodhpur, choose a blue-city guesthouse with Mehrangarh views — or a palace hotel if you’re splurging.
destinations.secTravel: Autos and cabs cover the cities; a hired car links Jodhpur and Jaisalmer. For the desert, camel or jeep safaris run from Sam and Khuri.
destinations.secActivities:
• Camel and jeep safari with an overnight in the Sam dunes
  • Explore Mehrangarh Fort and Jaswant Thada
  • Wander Jaisalmer’s havelis — Patwon Ki Haveli
  • Folk music and dance around a desert campfire
  • Shop the blue-city bazaars of Jodhpur
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Jaisalmer Fort (Sonar Quila) — the living golden fort
  • Mehrangarh Fort, Jodhpur
  • Patwon Ki Haveli
  • Sam Sand Dunes
  • Gadisar Lake and Jaswant Thada
destinations.secNotes: Bargain politely in the bazaars and agree safari prices upfront. Carry sun protection and a scarf for desert dust. Nights in the dunes get surprisingly cold in winter — pack a layer.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 6-day desert-Rajasthan run pairing Jodhpur and Jaisalmer.

  • Day 1: Jodhpur — Mehrangarh Fort
  • Day 2: Jodhpur — blue-city lanes & Jaswant Thada
  • Day 3: Drive/train to Jaisalmer
  • Day 4: Jaisalmer Fort & the havelis
  • Day 5: Sam dunes — camel safari & overnight desert camp
  • Day 6: Gadisar Lake, then onward
destinations.extFood:
• Dal baati churma — the Rajasthani signature plate
  • Ker sangri — a tangy desert-bean-and-berry dish
  • Gatte ki sabzi — gram-flour dumplings in curd gravy
  • Laal maas — fiery red mutton curry
  • Mawa kachori & makhaniya lassi — for the sweet tooth
destinations.extCulture: This is Rajput and Marwari heartland, rich in folk music — the Manganiyar and Langa musicians perform under the desert stars. Dress modestly, bargain with good humour, and aim for the Jaisalmer Desert Festival (February) for camel races and turban-tying contests.
destinations.extBudget:
• Heritage havelis: ₹1,500–5,000
  • Desert camps: ₹2,000–8,000 incl. safari & dinner
  • Daily budget: ₹2,500–5,000 per person
destinations.extFaq:
When should I go?
October–March only — summers are punishingly hot.

Is the camel safari worth it?
Yes — even a short sunset ride with an overnight camp is the highlight for most visitors.

How do I travel between Jodhpur and Jaisalmer?
An overnight train or a scenic 5-hour drive; they pair naturally on one trip.

destinations.name: South Goa
destinations.lead: The quieter, greener half of Goa — long empty beaches, swaying palms and Portuguese-era calm.
destinations.overview:
Where North Goa is party and bustle, South Goa is slow mornings and long, uncrowded sand. Palolem, Agonda and Patnem curve in golden arcs; inland, whitewashed churches and spice plantations sit among the palms.

It’s the coast for travellers who want the sea, a hammock and a plate of fresh fish — without the crowds.
destinations.secSeason: November to February is peak season — dry, breezy and warm. March–May is hotter but quieter. The monsoon (June–September) shutters many beach shacks but turns the hinterland brilliant green.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Goa (GOX/GOI); Madgaon (Margao) is the southern railhead on the Konkan line. Cabs and rentals reach the southern beaches in under an hour.
destinations.secStay: Beach huts and boutique resorts line Palolem, Agonda and Patnem. For heritage, choose a Portuguese-villa stay inland around Chandor or Cavelossim.
destinations.secTravel: Rent a scooter — it’s the Goan way. Cabs and app rentals fill the gaps; the south is compact enough to explore beach by beach.
destinations.secActivities:
• Beach-hopping: Palolem, Agonda, Patnem, Butterfly
  • Dolphin-spotting and kayaking from Palolem
  • Spice-plantation tours and Goan cooking classes
  • Sunset silent-disco and live-music nights
  • Day trip to Dudhsagar Falls (in season)
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Palolem Beach — the south’s signature crescent
  • Cabo de Rama Fort
  • Dudhsagar Falls
  • Old Goa churches — Basilica of Bom Jesus
  • Cotigao Wildlife Sanctuary
destinations.secNotes: Carry a helmet and licence for scooters — checks are common. Respect the calmer southern vibe: this isn’t a party coast. Watch for strong currents and swim between the flagged zones.
destinations.extItinerary:
A laid-back 5-day South Goa plan.

  • Day 1: Arrive — settle into Palolem
  • Day 2: Beach-hop — Agonda & Patnem
  • Day 3: Dolphin trip + Cabo de Rama fort
  • Day 4: Spice plantation & Old Goa churches
  • Day 5: Butterfly Beach by boat, then onward
destinations.extFood:
• Goan fish thali — the everyday classic
  • Prawn balchão — tangy, spicy and pickle-like
  • Pork vindaloo — the real Indo-Portuguese version
  • Chicken cafreal — green, herby and grilled
  • Bebinca & feni — layered dessert and the local spirit
destinations.extCulture: South Goa carries a relaxed sussegad rhythm and a blend of Hindu and Indo-Portuguese Catholic life — whitewashed churches, old villas and quiet feast days. Keep the southern beaches calm and litter-free; the big parties belong up north.
destinations.extBudget:
• Beach huts/resorts: ₹1,000–3,500
  • Scooter: ₹300–500 a day
  • Daily budget: ₹1,800–3,500 per person
destinations.extFaq:
North or South Goa?
North for nightlife and buzz; South (here) for quiet beaches and slow days.

Do I need a licence for a scooter?
Yes — carry your licence and a helmet; police checks are common.

When's the best time?
November–February for dry, breezy weather and open beach shacks.

destinations.name: Coorg
destinations.lead: Misty coffee hills, spice plantations and waterfalls — the “Scotland of India” in the Western Ghats.
destinations.overview:
Coorg (Kodagu) is a hill district of rolling coffee estates, cardamom forests and rivers born in the Western Ghats. The air smells of roasting beans and rain; the Kodava people are famed for their hospitality, martial heritage and distinctive cuisine.

It’s a soft, green escape — homestays on working estates, short waterfall walks, and slow mornings with the valley wrapped in mist.
destinations.secSeason: October to March is ideal — clear, cool and post-monsoon green. The monsoon (June–September) is lush and atmospheric, when the waterfalls run fullest. The altitude keeps it pleasant year-round.
destinations.secReach: Nearest airports: Mangaluru (~135 km), Mysuru (~120 km) and Bengaluru (~250 km). Mysuru is the closest railhead. Most travellers drive in via Madikeri.
destinations.secStay: Stay on a coffee-estate homestay or plantation resort around Madikeri, Pollibetta or Virajpet — the quintessential Coorg experience. Madikeri town has more budget options.
destinations.secTravel: A hired car or self-drive is best; the sights are spread across estates and valleys. Local buses connect the main towns but run infrequently.
destinations.secActivities:
• Guided coffee- and spice-plantation walks with tastings
  • Trek to Tadiandamol, Coorg’s highest peak
  • Visit Abbey and Iruppu Falls
  • Meet the elephants at Dubare Elephant Camp
  • Day trip to the Golden Temple at Namdroling
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Abbey Falls
  • Raja’s Seat — sunset viewpoint, Madikeri
  • Namdroling Monastery (Golden Temple), Bylakuppe
  • Talacauvery — source of the Kaveri
  • Dubare Elephant Camp
destinations.secNotes: Roads are winding — allow extra time and avoid night driving in mist. Try Kodava specialities like pandi curry and akki roti. Leeches appear on monsoon trails, so carry salt and cover up.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 4-day coffee-country escape.

  • Day 1: Madikeri — Raja's Seat sunset & Abbey Falls
  • Day 2: Plantation walk + Dubare Elephant Camp
  • Day 3: Golden Temple (Bylakuppe) & Nisargadhama
  • Day 4: Tadiandamol trek (or a slow estate morning)
destinations.extFood:
• Pandi curry — the famous Coorg pork curry
  • Kadambuttu — steamed rice dumplings to go with it
  • Akki roti — soft rice flatbread
  • Bamboo-shoot curry — a Kodava speciality
  • Estate-fresh Coorg coffee
destinations.extCulture: The Kodava are a proud, close-knit people with a martial heritage — one of the few Indian communities permitted to carry firearms without licence, and known for ancestor worship and distinctive weddings. Homestay hospitality is the heart of Coorg; the harvest festival Puthari is the year's high point.
destinations.extBudget:
• Estate homestays: ₹2,000–5,000 incl. meals
  • Daily budget: ₹2,000–3,500 per person
destinations.extFaq:
Best time to visit?
October–March for clear weather; the monsoon is lush and atmospheric if you don't mind rain.

Are there leeches?
Yes, on monsoon trails — carry salt and cover your ankles.

How do I get there?
Drive from Mangaluru, Mysuru or Bengaluru; there's no railway into Coorg.

destinations.name: North Sikkim
destinations.lead: Glacial lakes, alpine valleys and a blaze of rhododendrons beneath Himalayan snow peaks.
destinations.overview:
North Sikkim is the state’s wild, high-altitude frontier — a region of sacred lakes, hot springs and the spring-blooming Yumthang “Valley of Flowers.” Roads climb past 5,000 m at Gurudongmar, one of the highest lakes in the world.

It’s permit-controlled, weather-dependent and gloriously remote — Himalayan travel at its most pristine.
destinations.secSeason: March to June brings the rhododendron bloom and the clearest mountain views; October–November is crisp and dry. Winter snow often closes the high roads, and the monsoon (July–September) risks landslides.
destinations.secReach: Nearest airport: Pakyong (PYG) or Bagdogra. Railhead: New Jalpaiguri (NJP). From Gangtok, hired shared jeeps run to Lachen and Lachung with permits arranged by your operator.
destinations.secStay: Stay in the villages of Lachen and Lachung — simple guesthouses and homestays that serve as bases for the early-morning runs to Gurudongmar and Yumthang.
destinations.secTravel: Travel is by shared or hired 4x4 only, almost always as part of a permitted package. Foreigners need a Protected Area Permit; Indians need an Inner Line Permit.
destinations.secActivities:
• Dawn drive to Gurudongmar Lake
  • Yumthang Valley of Flowers and Zero Point
  • Soak at the Yumthang hot springs
  • Photograph Kanchenjunga and the snow peaks
  • Visit Lachen and Lachung monasteries
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Gurudongmar Lake
  • Yumthang Valley — Valley of Flowers
  • Zero Point (Yumesamdong)
  • Lachung Monastery
  • Seven Sisters & Naga Falls en route
destinations.secNotes: Permits are mandatory and arranged through registered Sikkim operators — solo travel to the high lakes isn’t allowed. Acclimatise in Gangtok first; Gurudongmar’s altitude affects many visitors. Carry warm layers even in spring.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 6-day North Sikkim journey (run as a permitted package).

  • Day 1: NJP/Bagdogra → Gangtok
  • Day 2: Gangtok — acclimatise, MG Marg & Rumtek
  • Day 3: Gangtok → Lachen
  • Day 4: Gurudongmar Lake at dawn → Lachung
  • Day 5: Yumthang Valley & Zero Point → Gangtok
  • Day 6: Departure
destinations.extFood:
• Momos & thukpa — everywhere, and excellent
  • Gundruk & sinki — fermented greens, in soups
  • Phagshapa — pork with radish and dried chillies
  • Sael roti — a ring-shaped rice bread
  • Tongba — warm millet beer, sipped through a straw
destinations.extCulture: Sikkim's Nepali, Bhutia and Lepcha communities give it a layered Buddhist-Hindu culture, dotted with prayer-flag-strung monasteries. It's also India's first fully organic state — respect its strict eco-rules. Festivals like Losar, Saga Dawa and Pang Lhabsol fill the calendar.
destinations.extBudget:
• Package-based: ₹2,500–4,500 per day including permits, jeep and stays
  • Village homestays: simple and warm in Lachen/Lachung
destinations.extFaq:
Do I need permits?
Yes — North Sikkim is permit-controlled and must be booked through a registered operator; solo travel to the high lakes isn't allowed.

How high is Gurudongmar?
Over 5,000 m — acclimatise in Gangtok first and go easy.

Best season?
March–June for rhododendrons; October–November for clear skies.

destinations.name: Munnar Tea Country
destinations.lead: Endless emerald tea gardens rolling over the High Ranges of Kerala’s Western Ghats.
destinations.overview:
Munnar is a hill station carpeted in some of the highest tea estates in the world — corrugated green hills, colonial-era plantations and cool, misty air. Once a British summer retreat, it’s now Kerala’s most photogenic upland escape.

Beyond the tea, the surrounding Western Ghats hold shola forests, waterfalls and the rare Nilgiri tahr in Eravikulam National Park.
destinations.secSeason: September to March is the prime window — clear, cool and green. Visit between August–October for misty drama, or time a once-in-twelve-years trip with the Neelakurinji bloom that turns the hills blue.
destinations.secReach: Nearest airport: Kochi (COK), ~110 km / 4 hrs away. Aluva and Ernakulam are the nearest railheads. The drive up through Adimali is gorgeous.
destinations.secStay: Choose a tea-estate bungalow or plantation resort for the views, or a budget homestay in Munnar town. Many stays sit amid the gardens with sweeping valley vistas.
destinations.secTravel: A hired cab or self-drive works best for the scattered viewpoints and estates. Autos cover the town; the roads are winding but well-surfaced.
destinations.secActivities:
• Tea-estate walks and a visit to the Tea Museum
  • Wildlife spotting in Eravikulam National Park
  • Boating on Mattupetty and Kundala lakes
  • Drive to Top Station for sea-of-cloud views
  • Trek towards Anamudi, South India’s highest peak (seasonal)
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Eravikulam National Park — Nilgiri tahr and Anamudi
  • Top Station viewpoint
  • Mattupetty Dam & Lake
  • Tea Museum, Munnar
  • Attukal & Lakkam Waterfalls
destinations.secNotes: Eravikulam closes during the tahr calving season (roughly February–March) — check before planning. Mornings are chilly; carry a light jacket. Book estate stays early in peak months.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 4-day tea-country itinerary.

  • Day 1: Kochi → Munnar (Cheeyappara Falls en route)
  • Day 2: Eravikulam National Park & the Tea Museum
  • Day 3: Top Station, Mattupetty Dam & Echo Point
  • Day 4: Kolukkumalai sunrise, then return
destinations.extFood:
• Kerala sadya — the banana-leaf feast
  • Kappa & meen curry — tapioca with fish curry
  • Nadan beef fry — a Kerala hills favourite
  • Appam with stew
  • Cardamom & estate-fresh tea
destinations.extCulture: Munnar's character was shaped by its colonial-era tea plantations, worked by Tamil and Malayali communities whose settlements still dot the hills. Old CSI churches and quiet estate roads set the tone. Onam brings the whole region to life with feasts and flowers.
destinations.extFaq:
When are the views best?
September–March; avoid peak monsoon if you want clear hills.

Is Eravikulam always open?
No — it closes for the tahr calving season, roughly February–March, so check ahead.

What is the Neelakurinji bloom?
A rare blue wildflower that carpets the hills once every twelve years — the next big draw worth planning around.

destinations.name: Lakshadweep
destinations.lead: India’s quietest islands — turquoise lagoons, coral atolls and barefoot calm in the Arabian Sea.
destinations.overview:
Lakshadweep is a scattering of tiny coral atolls off the Kerala coast — India’s smallest union territory and one of its least-visited. The lagoons glow an unreal turquoise, the reefs are pristine, and the pace is utterly unhurried.

Permits and limited access keep it exclusive; only a few islands such as Agatti, Bangaram, Kadmat and Minicoy open to visitors.
destinations.secSeason: November to April brings calm seas, clear skies and excellent diving visibility. The monsoon (May–September) makes sea travel rough and most resorts close.
destinations.secReach: Fly into Agatti (AGX) from Kochi, then transfer by boat to neighbouring islands. Some packages travel by ship from Kochi. An entry permit is mandatory for every visitor.
destinations.secStay: Options are limited and book out fast — resorts and government tourist huts on Agatti, Bangaram and Kadmat, plus the Samudram ship packages. Plan well ahead.
destinations.secTravel: Inter-island movement is by boat, arranged through your package. There’s little independent transport — most visits run as organised tours.
destinations.secActivities:
• Scuba diving and snorkelling on untouched reefs
  • Kayaking and glass-bottom boat rides in the lagoons
  • Lazing on Bangaram’s sandbars
  • Visiting Minicoy’s lighthouse and tuna villages
  • Sunset dhoni sailing
destinations.secLandmarks:
• Bangaram Atoll
  • Agatti Lagoon
  • Kadmat Island — diving base
  • Minicoy (Maliku) and its lighthouse
  • Pitti Bird Sanctuary
destinations.secNotes: An entry permit is required and arranged via approved operators — there’s no walk-in tourism. Alcohol is restricted (Bangaram is the exception). Pack reef-safe sunscreen and respect the strict no-coral-collection rules.
destinations.extItinerary:
A 5-day island package (the usual way to visit).

  • Day 1: Kochi → Agatti by air, transfer to your island
  • Day 2: Agatti lagoon — snorkelling & diving
  • Day 3: Day trip to Bangaram's sandbars
  • Day 4: Kadmat — diving, kayaking, reef walks
  • Day 5: Return via Agatti
destinations.extFood:
• Tuna (mas) — the island staple, in countless forms
  • Coconut-based fish curries
  • Octopus fry — a local delicacy
  • Mas huni-style breakfasts — shredded tuna with coconut
  • Fresh reef fish, grilled simply
destinations.extCulture: Lakshadweep's culture is Malayali and Muslim-majority, with its own Jeseri dialect and a gentle, unhurried rhythm. Dress modestly, note that alcohol is restricted (Bangaram is the exception), and remember tourism is permit-controlled to protect the fragile reefs.
destinations.extBudget:
• Packages: ₹25,000–60,000 for 4–5 days including permits, transfers and stay
  • Independent travel: very limited — most visits are organised tours
destinations.extFaq:
Do I need a permit?
Yes — an entry permit is mandatory and arranged through approved operators; there's no walk-in tourism.

How do I get there?
Fly to Agatti from Kochi (limited flights), then transfer by boat; some packages sail by ship.

Is alcohol available?
Only on Bangaram Island — the inhabited islands are dry.

travelTips.title: How to Plan a Trip
travelTips.imageAlt: A map, notebook and pencil laid out for planning a trip
travelTips.body:
Start with the season, not the place. The same destination can be a different trip from one month to the next — Ladakh is at its best from roughly June to September, the Kerala backwaters are calmest after the monsoon, and Rajasthan is most comfortable from October to March. Choose your travel window first, then shortlist the places that shine in it.

Set a budget with room to breathe. Add up transport, stays, food and entry fees, then keep 10–15% aside for what no itinerary predicts: a missed connection, a day of rain, a guide worth hiring.

Plan fewer stops and stay longer. Every change of base costs half a day of packing and transit. Two or three bases with day trips usually beat a new hotel every night, and they leave space for the places you only discover once you arrive.

Book the bottlenecks early; keep the rest flexible. Long-distance trains, flights and peak-season stays sell out first, and some regions — parts of Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, for example — need permits arranged in advance. Leave meals and most activities open.

travelTips.title: What to Pack for a Trip
travelTips.imageAlt: A backpack, flip-flops, shorts and swimwear laid out on sand, ready to pack
travelTips.body:
Pack for the weather you'll actually get. Check the forecast for every stop, not just the first. Mountains swing from warm afternoons to near-freezing nights, and coastal humidity makes cotton slow to dry — layers handle both better than bulk.

Build a capsule, not a wardrobe. Choose clothes in a few colours that all work together, plan to re-wear, and allow for laundry. Carry something that covers shoulders and knees for temples, gurdwaras and mosques.

Keep essentials within reach. Your day bag should hold ID, medicines, a charger, a water bottle and a change of clothes, so a delayed checked bag is an inconvenience rather than a crisis.

Leave room on the way out. Packing cubes keep things findable, and a bag that isn't full on departure means you won't be choosing between a handloom shawl and your shoes on the way home.

travelTips.title: Tech & Gear for a Trip
travelTips.imageAlt: Travel essentials laid out flat: camera, phone, tablet, sunglasses and a bag
travelTips.body:
Plan your power first. A 10,000–20,000 mAh power bank, a multi-port charger and a spare cable cover most trips. Power banks belong in your cabin bag — airlines don't allow them in checked luggage. India uses Type C, D and M sockets, so visitors should pack a universal adapter.

Make your phone work offline. Download maps, translation packs, tickets and boarding passes before you lose signal. In the mountains and on long rail journeys, connectivity can disappear for hours at a time.

Protect what you carry. Back up photos whenever you're on Wi-Fi, switch on device-location tracking, and use a padded sleeve or dry bag for cameras around water, sand and dust.

Bring only the gear you'll use. A phone with a good camera is enough for most travellers. If you do carry a dedicated camera, one versatile lens and a light tripod usually earn their weight; the rest can stay home.

travelTips.title: Travel Safety Tips
travelTips.imageAlt: A traveller with a backpack walking along a busy city street
travelTips.body:
Share your plans. Leave your itinerary and stay details with someone at home and check in at agreed times, especially before treks, long drives or trips into areas with patchy signal.

Keep valuables spread out. Split cash and cards between your wallet, your day bag and your room, carry a photocopy of your ID, and keep the originals secure. Use lockers where your stay offers them.

Choose transport carefully. Use registered taxis, app-based cabs or prepaid airport counters, agree the fare before you set off, and avoid arriving somewhere unfamiliar late at night when you can.

Know who to call. In India, 112 is the single emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Save it with your stay's phone number — and, if you're visiting from abroad, your embassy or consulate.

travelTips.title: Safety & Insurance
travelTips.imageAlt: A first aid kit with medicines and a stethoscope
travelTips.body:
Buy cover when you book, not when you leave. Cancellation benefits usually apply only to events that happen after you've bought the policy, so the earlier you buy it, the more of your trip it protects.

Read what's actually covered. Check the medical limits, emergency evacuation, trip cancellation and lost or delayed baggage. Adventure activities such as high-altitude trekking, scuba diving and rafting are often excluded unless you add them.

Carry a small medical kit. Keep prescription medicines in their original packaging with a copy of the prescription, plus basics like oral rehydration salts, antiseptic, plasters and motion-sickness tablets. At altitude, give yourself time to acclimatise.

Keep your policy within reach. Save the policy number and the insurer's 24-hour helpline on your phone and on paper. If you need treatment, call them first where you can — many claims depend on it.

travelTips.title: Visa & Passports Tips
travelTips.imageAlt: A passport open to pages of visa stamps
travelTips.body:
Check your passport's validity first. Many countries require it to be valid for at least six months beyond your return date, with blank pages for entry stamps. Renewals can take weeks, so check before you book anything.

Confirm the visa you need — including in transit. Requirements depend on your nationality and your route, and even a layover can call for a transit visa. Always check the destination's official government or embassy website rather than forums.

Apply early and keep copies. Where an e-visa is available it's usually the quickest route, but still leave time. Keep digital and paper copies of your passport, visa and bookings, stored separately from the originals.

Match your documents exactly. The name on your tickets, visa and bookings should match your passport exactly. A small mismatch can mean being refused boarding.

travelTips.title: How to Work Remotely and Travel
travelTips.imageAlt: Working on a laptop at a café table by the window
travelTips.body:
Test the connection before you commit. Ask your stay for a recent speed test, read reviews that mention Wi-Fi, and keep a mobile data plan as backup. Coworking spaces in cities and popular hubs such as Goa and Rishikesh make a reliable fallback.

Slow down. Staying a week or more in one place makes work predictable, and long-stay rates are often cheaper per night. Save the travel days for weekends.

Protect your working hours. Agree core hours that overlap with your team's time zone, block travel time in your calendar, and keep one dependable setup — a laptop stand and good headphones go a long way.

Sort the admin before you go. Check your employer's policy on working from another location and whether your visa permits remote work — tourist visas often don't. Use a VPN on public networks and keep your work backed up.

legalDocs.title: Frequently asked questions.
legalDocs.deck: Answers to the questions we hear most often.
legalDocs.body:
General

Is Triplipi a travel agency?

No. We are an editorial discovery platform. We don't sell trips ourselves — we refer you to verified partners with full disclosure. Think of us as a guidebook with hyperlinks.

Do you charge for content?

No. All editorial content — destination guides, blog posts, Our Picks lists, gallery viewing — is free to read. We're funded by partner commissions, photography licensing, and display ads.

Can I trust the partners you link to?

Every partner in our network has been personally vetted by our team — usually by travelling with them, sometimes by independent verification. We disclose our commercial relationship on every link via a consent modal. We label "Sponsored" placements clearly.

Booking & Quotes

How do I book a trip?

Browse destinations, find a package that suits you, click through (with consent) to the verified partner, and book on their site. Or fill our contact form with what you're thinking about, and we'll write back within one working day.

Do you offer customised itineraries?

Yes — through our partner network. Request a custom quote via any package page or the contact form, and we'll match you with the best-fit partner.

Photography & Shop

Can I license your photography?

Yes. Visit the Shop to browse our archive. Select the items you want, request a quote, and we'll come back to you with editorial, commercial, and extended-license options. A subset of our work is also available for instant licensing on Shutterstock.

Do you accept contributor submissions?

We work with a small group of trusted contributors. If you'd like to be considered, write to editorial@Triplipi.example with your portfolio.

Account & Privacy

Do I need an account?

No. Triplipi can be browsed entirely without an account. Trip drafts and shop selections persist locally in your browser only.

How do I unsubscribe from the newsletter?

Every newsletter has an unsubscribe link at the bottom. Alternatively, write to hello@Triplipi.example and we'll remove you within 24 hours.

about.storyBody:
For years, every trip we tried to plan began the same way — searching the same five sites, reading the same recycled paragraphs, clicking through the same affiliate funnels disguised as journalism. We wanted something different: a travel platform that read like a curated guidebook, looked like a magazine, and behaved like a friend with local knowledge.

So we built it. Triplipi launched in 2024 as a small editorial project — three writers, two photographers, a list of 60 destinations we'd actually been to. Today we've indexed 450 places, partnered with 180 verified providers, and published more than 320 long-form stories. The original idea hasn't changed: depth over speed, and honesty about how we earn our money.
about.missionTitle: To make travel discovery feel less like research, and more like reading.
about.missionBody:
We believe the best trips begin with the best stories. Our mission is to be the first place a curious traveller turns — not for booking, not for prices, but for the kind of honest, considered, photographically-rich account of a destination that helps you know whether you actually want to go.

When you're ready to book, we connect you to verified partners — with full disclosure of every commercial relationship, every time. Slow travel deserves slow journalism, and that's what we try to make.
